Every year I teach Robot Learning (IFT 6163) at Université de Montréal and Mila, and every year the course leaves behind more material than any single student sees: slide decks revised after each offering, hours of recorded lectures, the explanations and examples that come up when students ask questions, and figures built to make one idea click. This book is an attempt to collect that material into a form that is useful to people outside the classroom.

## The Source Material

The book is built from three sources that already exist for each lecture. The *slides* are the canonical outline: they fix the order of topics, the figures, and the mathematics. The *lecture recordings*, from several years of the course, capture what the slides leave out: the intuition behind an equation, the reason one method replaced another, and the examples that only come out when explaining an idea out loud. The *figures* from the slides carry over into the chapters, and many have been redrawn so they read clearly on a page instead of a projector.

None of these sources is a textbook on its own. Slides are terse by design. Transcripts are informal speech, spread across multiple years, and rarely in the order a reader would want. The work is in combining them.

## Where AI Comes In

I use a number of AI tools to help with this process, including open models run locally through tools such as Ollama and llama.cpp. They process and summarize the lecture recordings, draft prose, and write code for the figures and the tooling that builds the book. For each lecture, the slides are combined with the transcripts from every year the lecture was recorded, and the draft follows the structure of the slides while filling in the explanations from the recordings. The mathematics is carried over from the slides rather than rewritten, and citations are restricted to references that already exist in the course bibliography.

That draft is a starting point, not the finished chapter. I read, correct, and revise each chapter before it is published, and the content, the choice of topics, and the way they are explained remain mine: they come from years of teaching this course. The AI does the part that would otherwise make the project impractical, which is turning dozens of hours of recorded speech into organized first drafts.

## Why Do This

A course reaches the students who take it. A book reaches anyone who needs the material.

The chapters, slides, and recordings are open: free to read and watch for students at any institution and for practitioners who are not enrolled anywhere. Each chapter sits next to the slides and recording for the same lecture, so a reader can move between reading, watching, and reviewing the slides as suits the material.

Written chapters are also easier to search, skim, cite, and return to than a recorded lecture. And because the book is generated from the same sources I update for teaching, improvements to the course flow into the book each year. Robot learning moves quickly, and a book that is rebuilt from living course material can keep pace with it.

## Errors and Feedback

This is a living draft, and some chapters are further along than others. If you find a mistake, an unclear explanation, or a missing reference, please [let me know](https://fracturedplane.com/). Corrections improve both the book and the next offering of the course.
